#2806. Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020

Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar.

"This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company.

Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem.

It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge, which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020.

Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence.

That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX.

With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits.

After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025.

Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar.

"There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," said Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP. The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said.

Anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus.

For a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said.

Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to."

"At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy said. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that."

Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation."

That's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic missed its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money."

Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The company looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to use alternatives from Amazon and Google as well. Anthropic said it generated $1.72 in revenue per dollar spent on computing power in the third quarter, up from 68 cents a year earlier.

"It is true that it required lots of capital, but when you dig in and you realize that capital is going toward compute, and this is the team that's positioned to use that compute in the most effective way, then we could connect those dots," Chahal said. He added that those metrics showed it was "going to be a very high-quality business."

Anthropic isn't the only big win for VCs this year.

Five months before Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, SpaceX hit the market in what, until this week, was by far the largest IPO in history. SpaceX, which Elon Musk founded in 2002, produced outsized returns for firms including Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz.

SpaceX and Anthropic alone will make 2026 a monster year for the venture industry, easily exceeding any other year in IPO proceeds. And investors in OpenAI hope appetite remains strong for trillion-dollar companies next year, as the ChatGPT maker is looking to 2027 for a potential offering.

IVP's Dash said that in his AI portfolio, "a lot of companies are starting IPO prep" even if it's only "year four, year five, year six since inception." He hopes to see at least half a dozen companies go public at valuations north of $10 billion each in the second half of 2027.

Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia has left the chip giant without a clear leader at a time when the company already faced heightened concerns about a slowdown in spending. Nvidia is a key investor in Anthropic and OpenAI and a critical supplier and financing partner for the entire AI industry, which is getting hammered across the board.

In January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after this month's midterm elections, which included the passage of numerous ballot measures that could stymie data center development. Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner predicted after the election that market dynamics would push Anthropic to price toward the lower end of its range.

Narasin said he wasn't even sure the company would get that far.

"I was concerned they'd delay," Narasin said.

That makes the outcome that much more impressive, he said, after Anthropic priced above its expected range and upsized the offering.

"This will be bedtime stories for years for future VCs," Narasin said. "There was a company that was created, backed by angels and later venture" that in a few short years "became the single biggest IPO of all history."

— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

#2805. 32 things we learned in NFL Week 11: 49ers leave no doubt as league's elite teams emerge

The 32 things we learned from Week 11 of the 2026 NFL season:

1. While Sunday night's matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings pitted the league's No. 1 offense against its stingiest (in terms of points allowed) and, arguably, most ferocious defense, the Niners left no doubt who's currently atop the NFL mountain with their resounding, blitz-beating, 35-10 victory in Mexico City. A lot can happen between now and Valentine's Day, but the side effects of the Santa Clara substation might be the only thing standing in San Fran's path to a third Super Bowl appearance under brilliant HC Kyle Shanahan.

1a. Minnesota hadn't allowed more than 23 points in a game this season ... domestically anyway. But this is the third time the Vikings haven't scored more than 10.

1b. Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, is going to be experiencing a lot more firsts in the coming weeks now that he's elevated to QB1 of the Las Vegas Raiders. Sunday brought his first start against an AFC West rival, first start on the road, first regular-season TD pass – first three actually – and first INT, a fatal pick-six against the Denver Broncos. But make no mistake, Mendoza continues to show flashes, kept his team in a game against an opponent likely to be in the AFC's Super Bowl mix and – most importantly – survived an early baptism by fire against the Seattle Seahawks and Broncos, who feature two of the league's most formidable defenses.

2. The number of TD passes reeled in Sunday by Kansas City Chiefs TE Travis Kelce, nearly four years to the day since he last scored multiple times in a regular-season game. K.C. boat raced the Arizona Cardinals 34-7 on Mr. Swift's big day.

3. Number of sacks registered by DT Jeffery Simmons in the Chicago Bears' 21-13 defeat of the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. That's five sacks in three games since Simmons came to Chicago in what could still prove to be the biggest deal of the season, Kirk Cousins included.

4. The number of TD catches San Francisco All-Pro TE George Kittle has in two Mexico City appearances in his career, including two in Sunday night's bashing of the Vikings.

4a. Also the number of starting quarterbacks the Cardinals and Baltimore Ravens have used this season.

5. Jacoby Brissett is the common denominator between those teams, dealt from Arizona to Baltimore before this year's trade deadline. However, he lost his second start in six days with the Ravens on Sunday … despite giving them every opportunity to win during a wild game in Charlotte, which the Carolina Panthers won 35-33.

6. The number of NFL teams that were off this week, aka "bye-mageddon" in fantasy circles – the Atlanta Falcons, Cleveland Browns, Green Bay Packers, Los Angeles Rams, New England Patriots and Seahawks all idle in the league's lightest scheduling week of the season.

7. The number of touchdowns the Dallas Cowboys scored in their 51-30 rout of the Tennessee Titans.

8. The number of possessions Dallas had Sunday, one kneel-down by QB Dak Prescott notwithstanding, Brandon Aubrey booting a field goal on the one legit drive when the Cowboys didn't find the end zone.

9. The number of international games the NFL staged this season, an all-time record, the final game abroad in 2026 played Sunday night in Mexico City's Estadio Banorte between the Vikings and 49ers.

9a. The Niners improved to 5-1 in international games − 2-0 this season − and their .833 winning percentage tops among teams with at least five appearances abroad.

10. The number of international games the NFL could play annually going forward, at least under the terms of the current collective bargaining agreement, which runs through the 2030 season. Said another way, expect 10 international games in 2027.

11. Back to the Cowboys, who won by three TDs … but still surrendered 30 points and 346 yards with DC Christian Parker not calling the plays. Both figures represent the second-best outputs of the season for the Titans, who entered Sunday with the league's second-worst offense. Also, add two-hand touch issues to Dallas' endemic tackling issues.

12. The number of consecutive regular-season games the Pittsburgh Steelers have lost in Philadelphia. They last beat their intra-state rival Eagles on the road in 1965, roughly 15 months prior to the first Super Bowl.

13. But you're bound to lose any time 42-year-old QB Aaron Rodgers is your leading rusher … with 29 yards.

14. The number of times Cardinals TE Trey McBride was targeted in Sunday's defeat at Kansas City. (He caught nine of them but only for 54 yards.)

15. The number of NFL teams new Arizona QB1 Josh Johnson has been a member of – he didn't play for all of them – but any veteran as wise as this 40-year-old knows feeding McBride is the best course of action when you join a new team with an All-Pro pass catcher.

15a. The number of TD passes Johnson has thrown in his 14-year career (though it's worth noting he was actually drafted in 2008, fifth round by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers).

16. Who says 347-pound Bucs NT Vita Vea doesn't have abs?

17. The jersey number, at least most recently, for QB Daniel Jones, fired by the Indianapolis Colts after they were smoked 26-3 by the Houston Texans on Thursday night. And while Jones' next NFL employer is already a subject of debate, is a guy only a year removed from an Achilles tear and fresh off football shellshock in Indy really the answer for anyone in 2026?

18. The number of starts Cousins could potentially make this season given his trade from Vegas to Minnesota may confer him an extra game rather than a bye.

19. The number of points Philadelphia scored in their 19-16 defeat of the Steelers, the second most the Eagles have posted since QB Jalen Hurts was lost for the season after Week 5.

20. Congrats to Philly for breaking a seven-game slide and also to third-year QB Joe Milton, who notched his first regular-season victory.

21. As for the Steelers? At least their loss to the Eagles wasn't a direct result of WR Makai Lemon (1 catch for 3 yards), whom Philadelphia EVP/GM Howie Roseman scooped from Pittsburgh with the 20th overall selection of this year's draft – one spot before Steelers GM Omar Khan planned to take him.

22. However, Pittsburgh might need another wideout for its Black Friday game against the Broncos if coach Mike McCarthy opts to discipline DK Metcalf, who was ejected in the third quarter of the Steelers' defeat at Lincoln Financial Field. Didn't matter much from a performance standpoint given Metcalf had one reception for 2 yards on Sunday.

23. The New York Jets (3-8) suffered a second straight devastating win at SoFi Stadium … in terms of their pending draft position. They beat the Rams there in 2020, despite entering the game with an 0-13 record – the victory effectively knocking them out of the Trevor Lawrence sweepstakes atop the 2021 draft. Sunday, they edged the Chargers 27-24 – meaning the Bolts (1-9) stand a much better shot at obtaining Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith at or near the top of the board … and/or holding the Jets hostage for draft capital given Gang Green's obvious need for a quarterback next spring.

24. The age of Detroit Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs, who scored two TDs on the ground in Sunday's 31-21 defeat of Tampa Bay. Gibbs now has 52 career rushing TDs, tying him with Lions legend and Hall of Famer Barry Sanders for the most in league history by a player yet to reach his 25th birthday.

25. The Panthers are the only current division leader that has been outscored on the season.

26. Yet along with the Niners, Carolina is also the only team in the NFC with a two-game lead in the divisional win column.

27. The Buffalo Bills, Broncos and Lions have all win six in a row, and the Cincinnati Bengals' heater could match that if they knock off the Washington Commanders on Monday night.

28. The Bears have won five in a row and have not trailed throughout that hot streak, which coincides with QB Caleb Williams' Week 6 return from his hamstring injury.

29. But as the playoff picture in both conferences begins to crystallize, much of the intrigue seems to be in the middle of the pack. In the AFC, for instance – and all due respect to the Ravens and Patriots, both without their QB1s – the Steelers, Browns and Texans will quite likely wind up fighting for the final two wild-card spots.

30. The NFC should provide more high-quality drama. While the NFC East and South will almost surely be one-bid divisions, the NFC North and West ought to create plenty of tension as their teams vie for the final five playoff spots – some quality clubs sure to be left behind. Wednesday night's matchup, the first the NFL has ever played on Thanksgiving Eve, will pit the Packers and Rams in a contest that could have serious ramifications come January.

31. As we approach Thanksgiving, many – some? – will also flash back to that Tryptophan-induced nightmare that was the Butt Fumble … which celebrated its 14th anniversary Sunday. Maybe the Jets beating the Chargers isn't so bad after all.

32. RIP, Tom Jackson – a great player, analyst and person, the outpouring of love, respect and grief from ESPN telling you everything you need to know.

#2803. How Asian countries are looking to prop up markets as AI downturn sinks stocks

Market regulators in South Korea, China and Taiwan have introduced new measures aimed at supporting markets, as a tech-fueled sell-off in the region spills into another week.

On Sunday, South Korea's finance ministry said it would prepare its securities-market stabilization fund for immediate activation. The fund, reportedly established in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic by financial firms and other institutions seeks to support markets during sharp downturns and is valued at 10.76 trillion won (nearly $8 billion).

The government also plans to relax listed companies' daily share-buyback order limits for three months, starting Nov. 24 and start a "special intensive monitoring period" to prevent illegal short-selling. Regulators will also track margin lending and forced liquidations.

South Korean stocks have seen wild swings over 2026 as investors piled into, then fled from its two tech heavyweights, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both critical companies in the AI supply chain. The benchmark Kospi index is deep in bear territory, down more than 46% from its June high.

The ministry said that it "assessed that volatility in domestic and international stock markets has significantly increased recently due to internal and external uncertainties surrounding the global AI and semiconductor industries, as well as U.S. interest rate hikes," according to a Google translation of the release in Korean.

However, Seoul also said that the mid-to-long-term growth expectations for the AI industry remain intact, and that "excessive anxiety is not a concern."

Taiwan, which is also exposed to the AI industry through Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and other tech firms, has also moved to rein in market volatility.

Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission announced Friday that short selling below the closing price was "completely prohibited," while making it an exception if used for hedging purposes by securities and futures firms.

"Investors must not sell listed (OTC) stocks or Taiwan Depositary Receipts at a price lower than the closing price of the previous trading day," the FSC said, according to a Google translation of the statement in Chinese.

Margin requirements for short selling will also be increased, and applications from securities firms to issue warrants for listing will be suspended, as the regulator aims to curb speculative activity.

In a similar move to Seoul, Taipei encouraged firms to buy back stocks, adding that the purchases will be included in the companies' environmental, social and governance scores if completed between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027.

The island's stock market is heavily dominated by its tech industry, most notably, chip manufacturing giant TSMC. The stock fell 15% last week, while the index dropped 17.5%.

While South Korea and Taiwan are looking to curb speculative trading to arrest the slide in their markets, Beijing is looking to encourage more leverage-based buying.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange said on Sunday that exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for margin-financed stock purchases to 80% from 100%, starting Nov. 30. That means investors will be able to borrow more for their stock market bets.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges also announced fee cuts, while Shenzhen proposed a market-making mechanism for its ChiNext board. The steps will help inject more liquidity into the market that has also born the brunt of the souring in tech and AI trade, with the benchmark CSI 300 index closing lower for 14 of the past 15 weeks.

Seoul's markets led losses in the region, with the Kospi down over 3.26%. Smaller losses were seen in mainland China's CSI 300, which declined 0.71%. The Taiwan Weighted Index, however, reversed earlier losses to gain over 2% on Monday.

#2802. NBC Turns Heads With Player Choice for Browns’ SNF Promo

The Cleveland Browns are heading for prime time next week and Deshaun Watson will be in the spotlight.

During Sunday night's broadcast of the Minnesota Vikings' game against the San Francisco 49ers, NBC put Deshaun Watson alongside Raiders rookie Fernando Mendoza in a graphic promoting the Nov. 29 matchup in Cleveland. The NFL moved kickoff from 1 p.m. to 8:20 p.m. ET.

Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick, was a natural choice for Las Vegas. Cleveland fans have seen networks go a different direction with their team. In August, NFL Network featured Shedeur Sanders on its graphic for the Browns' preseason opener against Chicago. Watson started that game.

"NBC just used Deshaun Watson and Fernando Mendoza to promote next week's Browns-Raiders SNF matchup," one fan wrote. "I believe this is the first time a national TV network has used Watson to promote the Browns."

"Deshaun Watson has played himself back into the good graces of the national media. NBC just previewed next week's SNF game vs Raiders with Watson on the graphic. The first few games of this season it was Judkins and Schwesinger on upcoming game graphics," another added.

Watson remains a polarizing figure, and he heard it from his own fans in the preseason when he replaced Sanders to start the second half against Buffalo. It was his first game in Cleveland since he tore his Achilles tendon against Cincinnati in 2024. After the 31-7 preseason loss, Watson reminded reporters that some in the crowd had cheered the day he got hurt.

"It's a little bit personal. I think that's a disrespectful thing," Watson said after the Buffalo game.

The backlash followed Watson to Cleveland after more than 20 women accused him of sexual misconduct during massage sessions. Watson denied wrongdoing. He served an 11-game suspension in 2022 for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy.

Browns coach Todd Monken sat down with Watson after the Buffalo game. When he revisited that conversation this week, Monken said he wanted to know whether Watson had been able to let go of the frustration he'd carried for years.

"It really wasn't about his physical traits. It was really where you are mentally and emotionally," Monken said. "I felt like our conversation was on point. I felt like he had let it go. He had, got it off his chest. I didn't see someone who was broken. I saw someone that was hurt. There's a difference. I think he was hurt. I don't think he was broken. And I think that was the first step in terms of, 'okay, where do we go from here?'"

Each of Cleveland's six wins has come down to four points or fewer. Watson led the go-ahead drive in the fourth quarter of every one of them.

Against Houston, he got the ball back with 1:40 left and the Browns trailing 24-20. His 30-yard completion to tight end Harold Fannin Jr. put the ball at the 5. Quinshon Judkins scored on the next snap with 53 seconds left.

The Browns would like to see more of that execution early. Cleveland went three-and-out to open the Houston game and fell behind 17-0.

At 6-4, the Browns have seven regular-season games left to evaluate Watson before making a decision about 2027. Monken said during the bye that he and general manager Andrew Berry had yet to discuss Watson's future. Watson was more direct when asked if he wanted to come back.

"Of course I want to continue to build on the legacy that I'm building. And, again, ultimately, it's up to the front office. It's up to Jimmy (Haslam) and Dee (Haslam). It's up to AB (Andrew Berry). It's up to coach Monken and the city," Watson said. "So, at the end of the day, all I can do is continue to play good football, win games, and then, again, let them figure out what they want to do for the future."

#2801. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2800. Cam Skattebo renews backflip celebration days after vowing to shelve it: 'It's hard to hold back from'

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo vowed in the aftermath of Aidan Hutchinson's season-ending celebration injury that he was done doing backflips. That promise lasted less than four quarters.

Skattebo iced New York's 23-18 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday with a run for a first down at the 2-minute warning that allowed the Giants to finish the game in victory formation.

When the play was done, Skattebo stood up and flexed. Then he did a backflip.

That was four days after Skattebo said this regarding backflips in the aftermath of learning that Hutchinson tore his ACL while jumping in celebration of a sack:

"It's hard to see," Skattebo said Wednesday of Hutchinon's injury, per the New York Post. "I'm saying yeah. Mentally, I'm like, 'I'm not doing that.' That ain't going to happen to me."

Per the Post, Skattebo reserved the right to renew his signature celebration "if we go to the playoffs or something."

Sunday's game must have fallen under "or something."

Skattebo doesn't have to look to Hutchinson as an injury reference point. He sustained his own season-ending injury as a rookie, a dislocated ankle that left him in fear that he'd need to have his foot amputated.

He, of course, did not lose his foot and was back to backflipping over the summer before returning to football — or he was trying, at least.

The backflip then made multiple on-field appearances prior to his vow to stop them. He was asked about the decision to renew the flip at his locker postgame.

"When energy calls for it, it calls for it," Skattebo said. "My teammates, I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team. I play this game with my heart and soul.

"When that happens, it's second nature and it's hard to hold back from."

Giants head coach John Harbaugh was also asked about Skattebo's backflip at his postgame news conference.

"He couldn't help himself, could he. "He' just couldn't help himself."

#2799. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warns Americans of 'bumps in the road' after tech outages

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Americans to prepare for "bumps in the road" after a set of damaging technology outages rocked air travel and systems like Microsoft Outlook.

Government officials have largely dismissed the prospects that the outages, which also slowed bank transactions, are linked to a coordinated or artificial intelligence cyberattack.

Clayton, however, said on CNN's "State of the Union" that outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their systems to adapt to the AI age.

"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said.

"You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot," he said.

Clayton's warning came as the U.S. prepares to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. A technology outage prompted a nationwide ground stop just over a week ago, which lasted for hours.

The Federal Aviation Administration said router upgrades caused a flood of data that led to the ground stop, and that there is no indication of a cyberattack.

Separately, Microsoft said the Outlook outage was caused by "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent delivered a similar message on CBS' "Face the Nation."

Asked if Americans should be concerned about the security of their financial institutions, Bessent said: "No, they shouldn't."

"The patches may cause a glitch," he said, referring to measures banks are taking to safeguard from AI. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."

#2798. Lakers share encouraging Austin Reaves injury update ahead of Jazz game

Austin Reaves was a full participant at Lakers practice on Sunday after missing four straight games because of a left heel bruise.

The Lakers didn't do any live-action drills Sunday, but they did two sets of defensive breakdowns and two sets of offensive breakdowns.

"He did everything, making progress," Redick said.

Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a free throw against the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, at Fiserv Forum in Milwaukee. NBAE via Getty Images

Redick said Friday that Reaves would "hopefully" return over the next two games. The Lakers play the Jazz on Monday at Crypto.com Arena and the Spurs on Friday in San Antonio.

Reaves, who suffered the injury on Nov. 11 and has been day-to-day since then, is averaging 24.7 points (51.3% from the field, 40.9% from beyond the arc), 3.3 rebounds and 4.7 assists for the Lakers, who are tied for the best record in the league (14-3) with the Spurs and 76ers.

Redick has called Reaves' injury a pain tolerance issue.

"He's made progress every day and they're doing a great job at figuring out like the most comfortable insert and the most comfortable shoe, finding that right combination," Redick said.

Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers reacts after a late second half 3-pointer against the Detroit Pistons in Detroit, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Getty Images

Redick can relate to Reaves' pain considering the coach suffered a bruised left heel when he was playing for the Clippers in April 2016.

Los Angeles Lakers' Austin Reaves drives to the basket against Milwaukee Bucks' Nate Ament during an NBA game Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Milwaukee. AP Photo/Aaron Gash

"We've played three-quarters of a game with the two of them both available [over the last seven games], and we've gone 6-1. And so, I think it's just a credit to the group sticking with it."

#2797. U.S. probes Megaspeed, Alice Huang as new figure emerges in Nvidia chip case

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, as a report identified one of her associates as a key decision-maker at the Singapore-based company.

Alice Huang, with whom ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly had a romantic relationship, was a key figure in Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia linked to the fallout surrounding the leadership shake-up.

"There is an investigation ongoing into her firm and into her," Clayton told ABC on Sunday, adding that, "Nvidia chips, they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants, that's why we're focusing on this."

Alice Huang's associate, Chinese national Li Ming, who is now out on bail in Singapore, was "deeply involved" in Megaspeed's activities and took part in major decisions, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Saturday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The Singapore charges against Li concern alleged false representations to Super Micro Computer, a U.S.-based firm with known links to chipmaker Nvidia, though Megaspeed is not named in those charges.

Last week, the Commerce and Justice departments said that the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over potential export-control violations. Their joint statement said Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security and Singapore law enforcement interviewed Huang during an on-site check in June 2025.

The Justice Department later took the lead in the criminal investigation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS on Sunday that the administration was seeking answers from Nvidia about its chip sales to China, including who oversaw compliance and which levels of the company knew about the activity.

Separately, The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang was in contact with an officer of a top Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 through fall 2026, citing people briefed on U.S. intelligence reports.

Bloomberg reported last week that the Justice Department is investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang helped smuggle Super Micro products to China.

Li faces five charges in Singapore, including two counts of fraud by false representation, along with allegations involving the operation of a company he controlled, unauthorized bank-account access and another company director's duties.

Prosecutors allege he falsely told Super Micro that the company would hold and lease the servers it purchased.

The Journal reported that Li is out on bail and that his case is ongoing. He was offered bail of S$1 million in March 2025. The Singapore charges do not name Megaspeed.

Earlier this month, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said that police had found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang committed offenses related to the possible inaccurate declarations under investigation.

The ministry said she was issued a stern warning for providing information that police assessed as knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role at Megaspeed. It also said Singapore had not investigated her for espionage.

Megaspeed has said it is a "legitimate and lawful business" and that Huang left the company in August 2025.

The scrutiny is set to intensify in Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2, respectively.

The committees said they want answers about Nvidia's role in allowing Chinese actors to access advanced chips and the involvement of a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

Speaking to CNBC's Squawk Box on Sunday U.S. time, Ryan Fedasiuk, a former advisor for U.S.-China Bilateral Affairs at the State Department, said that there was "still a lot we don't know" about the case.

He said lawmakers would likely focus on Nvidia's customer relationships and "who knew what at the company when."

Fedasiuk added that there was "a very good chance" investigators would find that people at Nvidia knew their products could be used for restricted purposes. He characterized the existing evidence as containing "multiple" smoking guns.

#2796. Who should Wales pick for autumn finale v Japan?

Wales head coach Steve Tandy, with one eye on the World Cup, vowed to rotate his side for Nations Championship finals weekend even before his side had faced Australia.

Hopes of an autumn clean sweep - something only achieved once in 2018 under Warren Gatland - were dashed by the Wallabies at the Principality Stadium on Saturday.

Wales dust themselves down before finishing the November campaign against familiar foes Japan on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

The Six Nations is not a time for experimenting, so it presents a rare chance to have a look at players in the countdown to next year's World Cup in Australia.

Wales spluttered to victory against Eddie Jones' side at the start of the month and will expect a more comfortable success at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

The fixture, a fifth meeting with the Brave Blossoms in 16 months, presents a chance for Tandy to test his squad depth.

Did beaten Wales still show they have come a long way?

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Eleven of Wales' players started against Japan, New Zealand and Australia - Blair Murray, Louis Rees-Zammit, Eddie James, Max Llewellyn, Sam Costelow, Tomos Williams, Nicky Smith, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Dafydd Jenkins and Jac Morgan.

It is fair to assume that plenty of big hitters will watch from the stands at Twickenham, after the mental and physical demands of the past fortnight.

"I can rotate the team and we'll still put in a performance. It doesn't matter who wears the shirt, we've got to perform," said Tandy.

"Whenever we put a team out, the objective is to win a Test match. That will be no different next Saturday."

The core of the first-choice team will remain in England after the Japan game and rejoin their clubs in the Prem.

Former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert urged Tandy to resist the temptation to give the frontline players a breather.

"We need to put our best team out. We really want to put a marker down against Japan," he said on the Scrum V podcast.

"It's an opportunity to really put Japan to the sword if we really want to take some momentum into the Six Nations."

The Japanese are stretched by injury and conceded 24 tries in defeats by England and Scotland.

Wales fielded the same starting line-up against Japan and Australia either side of the New Zealand victory.

Man of the match against the All Blacks James Botham went from the XV to missing out completely against the Wallabies, much to the frustration of his father Liam.

Botham's fellow Cardiff back-row forward Taine Basham and Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb suffered the same fate.

Versatile forward Taine Plumtree has proved his worth from the bench in the past two fixtures but might hope for a first Test start since Scotland in the third round of the 2026 Six Nations.

Tandy is spoilt for choice in the back-row and gave promising Exeter flanker Kane James a second cap off the bench against the Wallabies.

Wales have also developed depth at loose-head prop to the extent that strong-running Rhys Carre, Welsh Rugby Writers' Association (WRWA) player of the year after his Six Nations exploits, missed out against New Zealand and Australia.

Smith has started all three November Tests and Ospreys' Gareth Thomas has been strong off the bench.

Wales selected three uncapped players in their initial Nations Championship squad with Cardiff loose-head prop Rhys Barratt, who played against the Barbarians in the summer, joined by the Dragons pair of scrum-half Che Hope and centre Aneurin Owen.

That figure became four when in-form Scarlets wing Macs Page got a call-up due to Rio Dyer's hamstring injury.

Tandy has given first caps to nine players since taking the reins in the summer of 2025 and could hit double figures at Twickenham.

There are seven other players in the squad who are yet to feature this month.

Centre Joe Hawkins failed to get off the bench against the Wallabies, when he was also Costelow's cover at fly-half.

Hooker Liam Belcher, tight-head Keiron Assiratti, lock Seb Davies, wing Ellis Mee and wing or full-back Tom Rogers have had no minutes, while fly-half Jarrod Evans was called into the squad last week when Dan Edwards suffered an injury in training.

Reuben Morgan-Williams kicked the ball off to seal victory for Wales against New Zealand [Huw Evans Picture Agency]

Reuben Morgan-Williams scored a sniping try in the win against the Barbarians in June.

The Ospreys scrum-half will hope to wear nine on his back for the first time in a Test match on the return to Twickenham.

Wales have been reliant on world-class Tomos Williams, and his deputy Kieran Hardy faces a fitness race for the World Cup after a serious knee injury.

Morgan-Williams was called into the fray for the last quarter of an hour against New Zealand and was introduced just five minutes into the second half against the Wallabies.

"Reuben played a fair part of the game and did really well," said Tandy. "He was very accurate in what he did.

"Tomos had a tight groin and we will assess that, but we've got to find out about Reuben."

Wales are scheduled to name their team on Thursday morning.

#2793. Yemen's Houthis claim attacks on Saudi oil refinery as Trump warns of new strikes next year

Yemen's Houthis, backed by Iran, said Sunday that they had targeted Rabigh oil refinery in Saudi Arabia, in the latest sign of worsening hostilities in the region, as Iranian forces seek to pressure the U.S. into accepting its terms.

The Houthis said they has directly hit the infrastructure, though the extent of the damage remains unclear, Reuters reported.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said earlier in the day that it had "intercepted and destroyed" a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia's western region, which included some of the country's critical energy refining and export infrastructure.

Rabigh, about 165 kilometers north of Jeddah on the kingdom's western Red Sea coast, hosts Petro Rabigh, a major oil refining and petrochemical complex, developed by Saudi Aramco and Japan's Sumitomo Chemical.

Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Interior did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Gulf countries reported multiple attacks by Iran-linked forces over the weekend, even as the country's foreign minister said his government remains open to a negotiated end to the war. Bahrain authorities said an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility injured two people on Saturday.

The string of attacks mark the latest sign of escalation in the regional hostilities since the war between the U.S.-Israel and Iran began in late February, as negotiators have so far failed to agree on terms to end the monthslong war.

The conflict has drawn in countries in the Gulf region, disrupting energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which used to carry a fifth of the world's crude shipments prior to the war, pushing up global prices for oil and commodities.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported another incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman on Sunday, after two tankers were struck by unknown projectiles the day before. The maritime agency gave no further details about the incident, urging vessels to stay vigilant about the operational environment.

Tehran has indicated its intention to end the war with the U.S. through diplomacy, but President Donald Trump has dismissed Iranian proposals. Both sides have been in indirect communication via Qatar.

In an interview to Fox News on Saturday, Trump warned that he was inclined to order military strikes against Tehran next year, if the two countries failed to finalize an agreement. The president blamed the Iranian officials for stalling while escalating hostilities after the U.S. elections.

"They're more aggressive now than before the election," Trump said, describing Iranian officials as "professional tap dancers." "They talk all the time, all they do is talk," he added.

The president has previously said that Tehran wants a deal to end hostilities but not one that is "acceptable" to him. He has oscillated between favoring an agreement that would end the fighting and insisting that the U.S. does not need to rush into any deal and is not afraid of resuming more aggressive attacks.

The Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday after a two-hour meeting with visiting Qatari mediators that, "We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy," according to Reuters.

International benchmark Brent futures inched 0.22% lower to $92.35 per barrel in early Asia trading hours, while WTI crude was down 0.19% at $83.25 a barrel.

#2792. Wild Lose Out on Dylan Larkin

The Minnesota Wild tried their best to acquire former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin, but in the end, they came up short.

On Sunday, the Red Wings announced they completed a blockbuster trade with the Montreal Canadiens, one sending Larkin to Canada for a package of players, prospects, and draft picks.

Thus, Wild GM Bill Guerin has lost out on his No. 1 trade target.

The Wild had a standing offer on the table for Larkin, which is said to have included Danila Yurov, Ryan Hartman, and three first-round picks.

However, Red Wings GM Shawn Horcoff did not accept this trade offer from Detroit, and instead, he dealt Larkin to Montreal, instead.

On the one hand, this is obviously very disappointing news for the Wild, as they clearly wanted Larkin and made a big trade offer to get him. But on the other hand, the Wild may have been overpaying for Larkin based on their trade offer for him, so they may end up benefiting from Detroit not sending him to Minnesota and completing the trade with Montreal instead.

With Larkin now officially heading to Montreal, the Wild could instead pivot to Sidney Crosby, as the Pittsburgh Penguins may trade their captain with the team on track to miss the playoffs this season.

Crosby is 39 years old, so he's older than Larkin, but he wouldn't cost as much in trade assets as Larkin since his contract expires at the end of this season. So, if the Penguins do talk to Crosby about a trade, then going to a Stanley Cup contender like the Wild makes a lot of sense.

Other than Crosby, there are certainly going to be some other top-end centers available on the market heading into this year's NHL trade deadline, so don't count out the Wild from finding their second-round center just yet.

The team still has plenty of assets to trade away in a deal, so look for Guerin to keep making calls to try and find someone to beef up their lineup.

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

#2784. Seattle Mariners Free Agency: How Tarik Skubal Deal Impacts Mariners' Pursuit of Seiya Suzuki

On Sunday, a new record was set in MLB free agency.

The New York Mets signed two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal to a nine-year, $450 million deal with a $45 million signing bonus, a new mark for the highest contract for a pitcher in MLB history.

Skubal joining the Mets doesn't have any surface level impact on the Seattle Mariners, who are set on their starting rotation for 2027 after dealing Bryce Miller to the Kansas City Royals for third baseman Maikel Garcia.

However, the Mariners are targeting outfielder Seiya Suzuki and Skubal's deal could have ripple effects that impact the team's pursuit of the right-handed hitter.

Among the other teams that have been reported as interested in signing Suzuki, who's projected to earn a four- or five-year deal worth more than $22 million a year, have been the San Diego Padres, Toronto Blue Jays and Philadelphia Phillies, among others.

The Blue Jays were the only team interested in Skubal that had also been reported to have interest in Suzuki.

Toronto was plagued with injuries to the starting rotation last season, and that seems to be the biggest priority for the team this offseason.

MLB insider Jon Morosi confirmed a report from MLB.com's Keegan Matheson that, with Skubal now off the board, the team is prioritizing signing Freddy Peralta.

The Blue Jays were rumored to have offered a nine-year, $400 million deal to Skubal, just under his final agreement with New York.

Peralta will command a cheaper deal than the two-time Cy Young winner, which will leave Toronto with more resources to pursue Suzuki.

However, the Blue Jays also have desires to add to the bullpen, which has seen the most activity this free agency.

Toronto has also been reported to be interested in third baseman/outfielder Teruaki Sato, who was posted by the Hanshin Tigers in Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball this offseason.

Sato is also projected to earn less than Suzuki, and the Blue Jays could be inclined to pursue the cheaper position hitter to sign both Peralta and multiple relievers.

The Phillies' interest in Suzuki has been in debate among insiders and reporters and other potential top-spenders haven't been reported to have any desire to sign him.

If Philadelphia isn't interested in joining the sweepstakes for Suzuki, and Toronto opts to chase after Sato instead, that would leave the Padres as the only other team competing with the Mariners to land the former.

On paper, Seattle likely wouldn't be able to outspend either the Phillies or the Blue Jays. The Padres' new ownership and several long-term, high-paying contracts on the team could end a more financially favorable bidding war opponent for the Mariners.

#2776. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2773. Ravens Report Card, Week 11: Mistakes and miscues mount in sixth straight loss

The Baltimore Ravens dropped their fifth consecutive game on Monday night, losing to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers by three points (23-20). Here are report card grades for the team's position groups from another disheartening defeat in Week 10.

Jacoby Brissett made a number of good throws in this game and orchestrated five scoring drives. It was not his fault that the Ravens fumbled the ball multiple times and his pass-catchers dropped more than five passes. The veteran finished with a 24-of-37 passing line with 276 yards through the air. His touchdown pass came via a trick play to a wide-open Rashod Bateman for a 25-yard strike in the fourth quarter. The Ravens may not have ultimately gotten down the field into position for a game-winning field goal, but there was time left to do so and Brissett's interception cost them that opportunity.

It's difficult to give a poor grade to the running backs when Derrick Henry and Justice Hill combined for 163 rushing yards, averaged over nine yards per carry and scored two combined touchdowns. However, while both were effective churning out yards on the ground, they also each lost a fumble. Hill's fumble at the goal line negated a would-be long touchdown run in the first half that instead resulted in a touchback. Then, in the fourth quarter with the Ravens trailing by six points, Henry had the ball poked out after making a screen catch. It was a controversial call that maybe should have been ruled an incompletion, but nevertheless Henry's ball security needs to be better. Fortunately, the Panthers did not score points off either of these turnovers — but they still costed the Ravens valuable points and possessions.

Zay Flowers had his most productive performance in several weeks, reeling in a team-high eight receptions on 11 targets for 97 yards. He was open a lot and created yards in space on crossing routes, which has been Flowers' bread and butter this season. He did have one drop just before halftime that would have been a long gain. Rashod Bateman started hot with 67 yards and a long touchdown catch early in the game, but only finished with two catches on six targets. Devontez Walker had a nice 34-yard grab on his only target. It was a quiet outing for Ja'Kobi Lane who was not credited with a target after receiving the most throws his way of anyone last week. Lane did draw an offensive pass interference in the first quarter but didn't see another look after that.

Mark Andrews was not able to replicate his season-best performance from last week, as he caught just two passes for 14 yards in this game. Matthew Hibner had an almost identical stat line while Josh Cuevas caught only one reception for eight yards. The tight ends collectively seemed to have a much more positive impact in the run game but failed to do anything more than minimal complimentary work as pass-catchers.

This was definitely one of the offensive line's better games this season — if not the best. They finally had a breakthrough showing in the run game, where they consistently won at the line of scrimmage and opened up big rushing lanes. The Ravens ran for 157 yards as a team and averaged 7.1 yards per carry, which was negatively skewed by one -13 yard attempt from Flowers that was blown up. In pass protection, the Panthers did have two sacks and six quarterback hits, so it was far from perfect. Brissett bought some extra time in the pocket, but also had a decent amount of time to throw on most of his dropbacks it seemed.

For the second straight week, the Ravens didn't do a great job stopping the run. The Panthers were able to rack up nearly 150 rushing yards and averaged 4.2 yards per carry. Chuba Hubbard scored twice and had a long 26-yard run. Travis Jones made some more impact plays with eight total tackles, one sack and one tackle for loss, while Calais Campbell had a quarterback hit and key third-down pass knockdown in the fourth quarter. The Ravens still do not generate enough consistent quarterback pressure through the interior, which is even more true without Nnamdi Madubuike in the lineup.

It was another standout outing from Mike Green, who continues to ascend in his sophomore season. Green had four solo tackles with two sacks, two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits. On the other side of the defensive front, Trey Hendrickso came close to recording his third sack of the season but came up short. Hendrickson did have a quarterback hit and tackle for loss, but he was also flagged for a clear roughing the passer penalty. The Ravens have unfortunately not been getting many splash plays from rookie Zion Young.

The Ravens' starting linebacker duo put forth another middling overall game. Trenton Simpson had a team-high 10 tackles and Roquan Smith had nine tackles with one quarterback hit. While the counting stats are fine, their impact defending the run was evidently not there consistently. Smith was notably beaten a couple times in man coverage, including on a third-down conversion late in the fourth quarter against Tommy Tremble.

Nate Wiggins seemed to have a solid game without his name being called much. Starting in place of Marlon Humphrey was Chidobe Awuzie, who gave up a few catches in the first half alone including a touchdown in the red zone. T.J. Tampa saw expanded snaps as an outside corner and made two impressive plays on back-to-back reps in the second half. He broke up a short pass attempt in the red zone and then intercepted Bryce Young's third-down throw that could have been a touchdown. Tampa also was beaten on a trick-play touchdown, but it was nice to see him come up with a turnover. Nickel corner Keyon Martin made a big open-field stop against Tet McMillan late in the game.

Kyle Hamilton has uncharacteristically been on the receiving end of some long completions in coverage the past two weeks. He was beaten by Jalen Coker for a 35-yard grab in the first quarter and the Panthers quickly scored a touchdown afterwards. He was also stiff-armed by Hubbard on a tackle attempt — also uncharacteristic. He did have eight tackles and one tackle for loss. Malaki Starks also had a tackle for loss but appeared to be somewhat at fault for coverage issues as well on a few plays. Backup K'Von Wallace had a career-high seven tackles.

Devontez Walker made the biggest play of the game for the Ravens, returning a kickoff 86 yards to the house for a touchdown. That second-quarter splash gave the Ravens a temporary five-point lead and big momentum lift. Another positive was Riley Patterson making his lone field goal and four extra point tries. This grade is low because of LaJohntay Wester, who muffed two punts and lost one of them. The Panthers scored a go-ahead touchdown directly off of the fumbled punt that they recovered. He was fortunate to not have lost both, although the second was recovered by the Ravens at the one yard line and created terrible field position.

#2771. “I feel like swearing”: Roy Keane rips into his former side after Liverpool debacle

Manchester United crashed and burned at Anfield, losing 4-0 versus their bitter rivals.

Leny Yoro was sent off after just eight minutes when he took down Alexander Isak as the last man.

Dominik Szoboszlai fired in the resulting free-kick and Florian Wirtz added a second to put United 2-0 down after just 15 minutes, and the game was as good as over early on.

This means that United are 19th in the table with one win from 11 matches this season in the league.

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Keane was less than impressed by his former side's efforts at Anfield in spite of going down to ten men early on.

He explained, "if you do the basics right, you give yourself a bit of a chance so no matter how good you think you might be or a big club you are, if you're not doing the basics right, you're going to be constantly under pressure and constantly getting criticised."

He added, "if that happened against a pub team, they'd be criticising you and this is a big game. You're talking about starting well, being solid, but again, we go back to the defensive shape and one stray ball over the top puts somebody in on goal. It's not good enough."

Keane continued to tear into the quality of his former side by explaining, "this team two years ago finished 15th. The last year or two, we're talking. We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers. When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making?"

He continued, "Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine, unbelievable chances they had. And everyone's coming off the pitch saying 4 is not too bad? I feel like swearing."

Keane also took aim at his former teammate and now colleague on Sky Sports, Gary Neville.

The Irishman snapped, "I thought United were desperate. So bad. Neville's ok with 4-0? Are you telling me they could have done better? 4-0 is not too bad with 10 men? Has anyone ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done! People who played for the club said 4-0 is not too bad? Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what? Performing rubbish."

United will need to react quickly when they take on Sporting CP in the Champions League on Wednesday night.

#2769. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2767. Barlow looks set for season debut with Sixers after long days, ‘miserable' weeks

Barlow looks set for season debut with Sixers after long days, 'miserable' weeks originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Dominick Barlow is on the verge of his season debut with the Sixers.

The team listed Barlow as probable for its Saturday afternoon matchup with the Bucks at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

Barlow practiced Friday and has been making clear progress in his recent on-court work recovering from an injury formally classified as a "lower back stress reaction."

He was a reliable rotation fixture last season, playing 71 regular-season games and starting 59. Barlow posted 7.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 0.9 steals per contest in 23.8 minutes per game. The Sixers then made a common-sense call to exercise his $3.4 million option for the 2026-27 season.

The 23-year-old described his back injury as "an overuse thing."

"I guess there was an area or maybe I started my (offseason) workouts too early," he said. "I don't know what it was fully in terms of what caused it. Once it happened, it happened. Nothing I can do about it besides try to correct it and get my body feeling as good as possible."

He called the past few weeks "miserable" as he rehabbed and waited on the green light by the Sixers' training staff.

"The days just felt longer," Barlow said. "Trying to be engaged mentally, which I think I've done a good job with, but the physical aspect wasn't there. I'm somebody that's prided himself on competing, being available. Not being able to do that was hard, but I'm excited to kind of put this past me."

With LeBron James and Jaylen Brown on the team now, Barlow won't start at forward when the Sixers are at full strength.

He's still a multi-dimensional frontcourt piece for Sixers head coach Nick Nurse who may very well get substantial opportunities at backup center.

"Just cutting, playing hard, being ready to make the open shot," Barlow said. "And then I don't think you can ever have too much defensive versatility. I think that's something I can bring, try to help us be more versatile."

When Barlow checks into his first game of the season, he'll appreciate the moment.

"You don't really realize what you have until it's not there (anymore)," he said. "I'm just excited to play. …. Just playing the first stint … that's going to be the main thing I'm looking forward to."

Dean Wade (left hamstring soreness/tightness)
