#2661. ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ review: Defense rules as Giants defeat Jacksonville

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants didn't do it the easy way, but they did manage to get a huge victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. Let's get to our 'Kudos and Wet Willies' review.

The defense as a whole — The Giants turned away the Jaguars again and again on Sunday, refusing to let a missed field, a Cam Skattebo fumble, and an inconsistent day from quarterback J.J. McCarthy stand in the way of a signature victory for the Giants as they improved to 6-3-1, and moved a step closer to their first NFC East title since 2011.

The Giants pressured a flustered Jacksonville quarterback Trevor Lawrence into his worst game of the season. Lawrence went 25 of 47 for 301 passing yards, but threw two interceptions, was sacked three times, hit 11 times, adn was chased endlessly by Giants pass rushers.

The Giants got interceptions from Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo. They had 14 passes defensed. They had a key fourth-down stop on fourth-and-1 at the Giants' 11-yard line late in the third quarter after a Cam Skattebo fumble had given the Jaguars the ball at the New York 31-yard line.

Abdul Carter — Flush with the excitement of a great performance in a huge victory for the Giants, Carter called himself "the best in the world."

Carter has a long way to go before he can prove that, but he might well have been the best pass rusher in the NFL on Sunday. Carter said he played "real angry" after seeing some online criticism over the fact that he entered the game with just 2.0 sacks.

Lawrence ended up feeling Carter's anger in the second-year edge defender's best game as a pro. Carter had two sacks, five quarterback hits, and a career-high 12 pressures, per NextGen Stats. This was the first multi-sack game of Carter's career.

Deonte Banks — Banks set up the Giants' first points with an interception that put the ball at the Jacksonville 31-yard line. He also had three passes defensed, including one on a desperation throw into the end zone by Lawrence on a fourth-quarter pass from the 12-yard line.

Paulson Adebo — The forgotten veteran cornerback was forced into action when the Giants lost starter Greg Newsome II to an ankle injury after just four snaps. Adebo was terrific.

Adebo intercepted a Lawrence pass with 11:08 left in the game, putting the Giants at the Jacksonville 28-yard line and setting up a Dominic Zvada field goal. Adebo also had four passes defensed. Per Pro Football Focus, he gave up just one completion in eight targets while spending much of his day chasing Jacksonville's Parker Washington.

Per PFF, his passer rating against was 0.0. Adebo got a game ball from John Harbaugh.

D.J. Reader — The big nose tackle's job is to stuff the run. He certainly did that Sunday with a tackle for loss and, per PFF, three stops. Somebody forgot to tell him, though, that nose tackles not named Dexter Lawrence aren't supposed to be impact pass rushers. Reader had a sack, two quarterback hits, and five total pressures. He continued to play at a Pro Bowl level.

Reader celebrated with a simple social media post:

Malik Nabers — I am honestly not sure about this one, but Nabers did have seven receptions for 55 yards and a touchdown. Through 29 career games, Nabers has caught 192 passes, the third-most through that many games in NFL history behind only Odell Beckham Jr. (199) and Puka Nacua (194).

Xavier Gipson — The Giants' new return man averaged 25.0 yards on five kickoff returns, including a 36-yarder, and had a 27-yard punt return. The Giants said they signed Gipson off the Philadelphia Eagles' practice squad because they needed "a spark" in the return game. Gipson gave them one.

Dru Phillips — Yeah, yeah. Phillips gave up seven completions on nine targets. Don't care. I care about his three passes defensed, especially on fourth-and-1 from the Giants' 11-yard line in the third quarter.

Jordan Stout — The Giants' punter averaged 60.3 yards on four punts, with a net of 54.5. The shortest punt Stout had was 57 yards. The amazing thing is that Stout manages to hit the ball that far while still getting enough hang time on his punts to give the Giants a chance to cover them.

Zaire Barnes and Tyler Nubin — Barnes had four special teams tackles, added to the league-leading 14 he had entering the game. Nubin has not sulked about losing his starting safety job to Ar'Darius Washington. He had three special teams tackles.

Second half offense — The Giants' offense seemed out of sorts after Cam Skattebo's fumble late in the third quarter with the Giants seemingly driving for what could have been a score that would have effectively put the game out of reach.

After that the Giants got just one first down over their next four possessions, netting -20 yards of offense along the way. They played oddly for a team trying to run the clock and protect a lead. Over those four drives, they ran the ball only one time. Those four possessions took a total of just 3:44 off the clock, and continued to give Jacksonville opportunities to get back into the game.

Micah McFadden — This was a rough night for McFadden. He made six tackles, and missed same number. Missed tackles have always been a bug-a-boo for McFadden, and this might have been his worst-ever game in that department. He missed a tackle in the backfield on a fourth-and-1 that went for a 21-yard run, and had a handful of chances to nab Lawrence in the backfield that he could not convert.

Cam Skattebo — Skattebo had a costly third-quarter fumble. He had just 34 yards on 14 carries, an average of 2.4 yards per attempt. After his third quarter fumble, the Giants seemed determined NOT to hand him the ball. Still, when the Giants needed a first down to ice the game, Skattebo delivered with two runs for 10 yards and a game-clinching first down at the two-minute mark.

Skattebo also delivered a trademark backflip, a move he said he had retired, after the victory-sealing first down.

"When energy calls for it, it calls for it," Skattebo said. "I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team. I play this game with my heart and soul. When that happens it's second nature. It's hard to hold back from."

J.J. McCarthy — This was not McCarthy's steadiest game throwing the ball. He went just 18 of 38 (47.4%) for 173 yards and a touchdown.

McCarthy overshot a wide open Darnell Mooney on a couple of deep throws. He missed Mooney on a deep out where he was open. He failed to see an open Malik Nabers for what could have been a long touchdown.

Yet, he made game-winning plays. His 8-yard touchdown pass to Nabers was a nice touch throw. He made a terrific 19-yard throw to Malachi Fields for a critical first down inside the three-minute mark. McCarthy used his legs to escape the pocket and pick up some key first downs.

His play of the game, though, might have been his touchdown-saving tackle of Antonio Johnson after the Skattebo fumble.

Dominic Zvada — The rollercoaster ride with the Giants' strong-legged rookie placekicker continued on Sunday. He made field goals of 53 and 54 yards — from the right hash mark where all six of his misses had occurred this season. Then, Zvada missed a chip shot 32-yarder from that right hash early in the third quarter before adding a 43-yarder from the left hash mark for three critical points with 10:03 to play.

The Giants continue to express faith in Zvada, but it can't be a surprise to anyone if the Giants work out placekickers some time soon.

#2660. Christian McCaffrey touchdown gives 49ers 35-10 lead in fourth quarter

It’s just about all but over in Mexico City.

49ers running back Christian McCaffrey capped a 13-play, 98-yard drive with a 6-yard touchdown to give San Francisco a 35-10 lead with 13:26 left in the fourth quarter.

Minnesota had put San Francisco on the 2-yard line with a well-covered punt. But San Francisco was nevertheless able to methodically make its way down the field, converting three third downs on the way to the end zone.

Newly acquired Keenan Allen caught two of the third-down conversions, moving the chains on third-and-4 with an 8-yard catch and on third-and-9 with a 13-yard reception.

The drive covered 7:04 across the third and fourth quarters, putting Minnesota in an even more unfavorable position as the team tries to get back in it.

McCaffrey now has 11 rushing touchdowns this season along with three receiving TDs.

#2656. Jazz vs Mavericks recap: A wild finish in Salt Lake City

It was looking like another depressing night for Jazz fans. The young Jazz were plagued with turnovers (20 by the end of the third quarter), Darryn Peterson was struggling from three again (he's 0 for his last 15), and more injuries started piling up with Jaxson Hayes leaving early and Keyonte George turning another ankle. And once again, the Jazz slowly watched the Mavericks' lead grow and grow to near-insurmountable odds.

Then Isaiah Collier came in, and it felt like the Jazz had thrown in the towel.

With the game seemingly over after the third quarter, Svi Mykhailiuk scored 23 points in the fourth quarter and went absolutely nuclear. For the game, Mykhailiuk had 39 points and shot 10/15 from three. With less than 10 seconds left, Isaiah Collier scored on a layup to tie the game. On a side note, it's great that Isaiah Collier also had a hand in this one. He's had a great attitude despite being benched, and deserves some credit for his energy and hustle.

Heartbreak ensued when Ace Bailey fouled Cooper Flagg with four seconds left in the game, and Flagg hit the free throws. Then, an inbounds play ended with Kyle Filipowski missing a three to finish.

Yes, it was a dissapointing end. And yes, it was depressing to see our young players struggle again on a night they probably should have done better. It was the back end of a back-to-back for the Mavericks, after all. But this felt like something that could carry over into the next game and the rest of the season. It probably built some confidence for the bench, or at least in Svi Mykhailiuk, and might be the thing that reminds the Jazz they can win these games even when things aren't looking good. At least that's what you hope.

If I'm Keyonte George or Darryn Peterson, I'm looking at what Svi Mykhailiuk did, and I'm learning from it. The reality is that Utah has had two truly explosive games this season, one from Brice Sensabaugh, and one from Svi Mykhailiuk. We've had some dominant nights from Keyonte George but haven't experienced consistent explosive play from the starting lineup. If there's one thing you hope for from this one, it's that the Jazz starting lineup can take the confidence Svi showed tonight and incorporate it into their own play.

Hey, it might even improve their turnover issue. Believing in their ability could mean that the other things fall into place more, we'll find out tomorrow when they take on the Lakers once again.

Are the 49ers the best team in the league?

#2652. Karl-Anthony Towns dominates Pacers in return to push Knicks’ win streak to five

Karl-Anthony Towns returned from an illness to carry the surging Knicks.

The center dominated the Pacers on Sunday night, finishing with 30 points and 13 rebounds in a resounding 113-106 victory.

It represented a fifth straight win for the Knicks (11-6), who pulled away in the third quarter because Towns caught fire.

New York Knicks guard Jose Alvarado (5) and center Karl-Anthony Towns (32) react after scoring against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Jason Szenes for NY Post

He scored 16 points in just nine minutes of the period as the Knicks went on a 20-11 run to take a 89-78 lead entering the fourth quarter. It ended with a nifty dribbling display into a 3-point conversion from Jose Alvarado.

Then Josh Hart helped close the win in the fourth quarter, earning a triple-double with 10 points, 11 boards and 10 assists in 39 minutes. Hart, who holds the franchise's single-season triple-double record, needed the confidence boost after riding the struggle bus to start the season.

Towns, meanwhile, has been consistently excellent.

A night earlier in a nail-biting victory over the Blazers, he was a DNP with an illness. Towns was then listed as questionable before Sunday's Pacers game, with coach Mike Brown claiming about 90 minutes before tipoff that Towns' availability was a game-time decision.

Turns out, KAT was fine. His biggest problem was foul trouble, which kept him on the bench for all but three minutes of the fourth quarter. Luckily, Hart and Jalen Brunson (22 points, seven assists) picked up the slack to put away the plucky Pacers (5-12), who stink again this season but always play tougher — and more motivated — against the Knicks.

Towns, 31, is giving the Knicks plenty of reasons to reopen negotiations on a contract extension. He has 16 double-doubles in 16 appearances.

Josh Hart #3 and Jose Alvarado #5 of the New York Knicks react during a game against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in New York. Getty Images

The Pacers were playing without Tyrese Haliburton, who has been out since last month with a hamstring strain. That didn't matter nine days prior, when the Pacers toppled the Knicks in Indiana without Haliburton.

This time, the Knicks were home and better.

The Knicks had their own injury issues Sunday. OG Anunoby missed his second consecutive game with soreness, although Brown downplayed the severity of the injury. Miles McBride was a late scratch with left adductor tightness, a new injury that's concerning only because of the area. McBride missed a couple months last season after sports hernia surgery, which is in the vicinity of his adductor.

The first half was tight throughout, with neither team leading by more than four points and the score a modest 55-51, Knicks advantage, at the half. It was a continuation of New York's offense this season being behind the defense, which is apparently a league-wide trend with scoring down across the NBA.

"I didn't know it was down overall," Brown said. "I don't know. I don't know if the defenses are getting better. I do know we, just our team, we haven't shot the ball as well as we'd like. But every game we're getting a little bit better, everybody's percentages are going up just a little bit every game, and that's exciting. I think eventually for us, right now our defense is way ahead of our offense, but our offense is coming, and hopefully we'll get there sooner than later."

Towns changed the tenor in the third quarter by hitting 5-of-8 shots, including 2-for-2 from beyond the arc. His return meant a DNP for James Wiseman, who played well in Saturday's win over the Blazers but is still the third-stringer behind Towns and Andre Drummond.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) shoots during the first half of a game against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, at MetLife Stadium. Jason Szenes for NY Post

Landry Shamet, whom Brown declared pregame as the clear frontrunner for Sixth Man of the Year, started again because of Anunoby's injury. He finished with 17 points in 32 minutes, including 12 points in the first half.

Hart looked like he was headed toward another frustrating night, appearing hesitant or even unwilling to take open 3-pointers. He had just two points at the half. But he picked up some momentum after the break, with the help of his podcast buddy Brunson.

Early in the third quarter, the two were running together on a breakaway, and Brunson, who had the open lane, bounced a pass to Hart for his first dunk of the season. It gave the Knicks a 12-point lead — their biggest of the night up to that point.

#2651. What NFL had to say about controversial call that took critical touchdown from Jaguars in loss to Giants

The football world is abuzz over the no-touchdown call on a fourth–quarter pass to Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington in Sunday's game against the Giants.

While it appeared that Washington had made the catch in the end zone with the Jaguars trailing the Giants 20-6 at the time, the officials ruled it an incomplete pass and confirmed the call after a video review.

The Giants went on to win the game 23-18.

New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips (22) defends against Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) on Nov. 22, 2026, in Brooklyn, N.Y. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

Everyone from Washington to the fans to CBS Sports rules analyst Gene Steratore all believed that Washington had control of the ball.

"I did not think he lost possession of the football. … I think it's a touchdown, fellas," Steratore said during the broadcast.

However, the NFL did not agree. In an interview with a pool reporter, NFL VP of instant replay Mark Butterworth said Washington did not have full control of the ball.

"The ruling on the field was an incomplete pass," Butterworth said. "First, to overturn a call, we need clear and obvious video evidence to overturn the on-field ruling. It was determined that the receiver did not gain full control of the ball until he was out of bounds."

In follow-up questions, he confirmed that he was referring to the fact that when Washington hit the ground, the ball was moving in the Jaguars receiver's hands.

Jaguars head coach Liam Coen told reporters after the game that the explanation he got was that "the ball switched hands, so that's what it came down to."

New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips (22) defends Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) during a game on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

Jacksonville had to settle for a field goal on the drive to only cut the Giants' lead to 20-9.

"I felt good about it, but they said it wasn't a catch, so had to move on and finish that game," Washington told reporters after the game.

#2650. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2649. Brock Purdy, MVP? 49ers, Super Bowl champions? It's all on the table now for San Francisco

For millennia, philosophers and professors have pondered an impossible question: What happens when an irresistible force meets an immovable object? Well, we have our answer, and we didn't even need AI to solve it: Irresistible Force knocks out Immovable Object by 25 points.

San Francisco and Minnesota arrived in Mexico City at the absolute pinnacles of the NFL's two barometers of excellence. No team in the NFL gains more yards per play than the 49ers. No team sacks opposing quarterbacks more than Minnesota. Dominating offense, smothering defense. Irresistible force, immovable object.

Or not. The 49ers strode onto the field at Estadio Azteca and proceeded to stomp all over the Vikings. San Francisco set the tone with an opening seven-play, 72-yard drive that finished in the end zone less than four minutes into the game. The Vikings struck back with an immediate answering touchdown.

And then, like a street fighter wiping a drop of blood off his lip before administering a generational beatdown, the 49ers simply blew away the league's top scoring defense with a total of 35 points, through the air and on the ground. And if you could score touchdowns by water, well, the 49ers probably would have done that too. This was a statement win carved into the side of a mountain, a declaration that the road to the Super Bowl runs through San Francisco.

At 9-1, the 49ers now lead the the NFC West by three games and the NFC as a whole by a game, and stand even with the Bills for the best record in the NFL. Aside from an inexplicable loss to the Falcons — who probably won't get another shot at the 49ers this season — San Francisco has overwhelmed its opposition at every turn.

If there's anything that can slow this 49ers team, it's the blue medical tent. Injuries have ravaged the 49ers all season, and on Sunday night, San Francisco ran out a Geriatric Avengers of thirtysomethings including George Kittle, Mike Evans, Christian McCaffrey, Deebo Samuel and Kyle Juszczyk. All that experience gives the 49ers a big-game-pressure edge that few teams can match, but it also makes them intensely vulnerable to injury. Stints on the IR are a when, not an if, for the 49ers.

The guy ensuring all those uncs get the ball is finally receiving some attention of his own again, too. Brock Purdy hasn't shown up on MVP leaderboards since finishing fourth in his breakout season of 2023, but this season ought to change that. He's among the league leaders in touchdowns, passer rating and completion percentage, among other useful stats.

Against the best defense in the NFL, all Purdy did was throw for three touchdowns and 255 yards on 21 of 26 completions. He's grown into the perfect weapon for head coach Kyle Shanahan's unorthodox offense, and Sunday was the perfect showcase.

"Brock, he didn't get rattled, which he really never does," Shanahan said after the game. "It's not like it's something new today to me with Brock. Brock's been like this since Day One, and he's played at a very high level for a number of years now."

Purdy and Shanahan wisely used the Vikings' vicious aggressiveness against them. The NFL Next Gen Stats chart of Purdy's completions tells the tale; virtually all of his completions were within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage, meaning he got rid of the ball so quickly that Minnesota couldn't catch up. You can't record a sack when the ball's already downfield.

"He just has this aura in the huddle," said Kittle, who caught Purdy's first two touchdown passes. "Everybody locks eyes with him, and we know every play, we have the chance to do something special."

"He's the best player in the game right now. He's super dialed in, the way he prepares, the way he competes," said Evans, who caught Purdy's third touchdown pass of the night, late in the first half. "He's tough. I always thought he's been underrated — his precision. Super-smart player."

This 49ers team is something special, and not just because they've already managed to win in three countries and two hemispheres this season. They're in the meat of their schedule now; the Seahawks, Rams and Chiefs all await over the next five weeks. But so too do teams like the Chargers, Eagles and Cardinals; San Francisco's schedule ranks 23rd in the NFL in terms of remaining difficulty, per Tankathon.

#2647. 'Tough on him, but we played the best attack' - Shubman Gill hints Mohammed Siraj might not play the 2nd Test vs NZ at Christchurch

'Tough on him, but we played the best attack' - Shubman Gill hints Mohammed Siraj might not play the 2nd Test vs NZ at Christchurch originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Shubman Gill defended the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the Wellington Test.

India's captain suggested that most of the side would stay the same in Christchurch.

A series locked at 0-0 raises the stakes for India's World Test Championship hopes.

Shubman Gill admitted that it was a hard decision to leave out "friend" Mohammad Siraj, but India picked the strongest attack available at the first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve.

The comments were widely read as a hint that the senior bowler may have to wait again when the second Test begins at Hagley Oval in Christchurch on Friday, November 27.

Gill made it clear that form, rather than reputation, had guided the selectors.

"We played the best attack for this match. Siraj's a really good friend and dropping him was a really tough call. We have played lot together and I know him since early days," Gill said.

He then spoke about a private conversation with the seamer, and how he could make a comeback into the team.

"I had a chat with him before the Test, explaining the call to him, and he understood that. See, every player will see a phase where they are not at their peak, and we picked on current form. A player can make a comeback by performing well," he added.

On the question of changes, Gill gave a clear indication that the side would not be altered much.

"In the second Test, the most of the team would be similar," Gill said.

He was also asked whether the presence of both Siraj and Ravindra Jadeja would have made a difference in the team. His reply was short and blunt: "I don't think so. For the seamers, there was nothing at all. Spinners got a little bit of help, but having said that, there was nothing much for the spinners either."

India's first-Test attack consisted of Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna, with off-spinning all-rounder Washington Sundar as the spin option. Siraj and Gurnoor Brar were both left out, a call Gill had called "a hard decision" at the toss on November 19, since "all of our fast bowlers have been doing really well."

Assistant coach Sitanshu Kotak and bowling coach Morne Morkel supported the combination. Kotak pointed to the height and bounce of the quicker bowlers on a damp, grassy first day, while Gill also wanted extra batting depth in the lower order through Kamboj and Akash Deep.

"There is nothing wrong [with Siraj]. I mean I can't see anything wrong," Kotak told reporters after the opening day's play in Wellington. "That's the best possible XI the team management thought and that is the one which played [this game]. Sri Lanka, obviously it was different conditions, and Siraj played both the Tests there."

"Obviously pace is one thing because when you are playing on a wicket which is a little damp, soft to start with, with a lot of grass, obviously one with height, which gives [extra] bounce [is an advantage]."

#2645. As Liam Coen explains Jaguars' late field-goal decision, Giants take offense: 'Disrespectful as hell'

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Down eight points with 3:43 to play, the Jacksonville Jaguars faced fourth-and-goal from the 8-yard line.

Should he bank on his offense, which converted just once on six red-zone trips Sunday, to reverse course amid unfavorable down-and-distance? Or should the Jaguars kick the 26-yard field goal, narrow their deficit to 5 points and trust the defense that held the New York Giants to 3 points in the second half to get a stop?

"Fourth-and-8 … what are those percentages of success? I think they're probably less than 5 [percent] in a lot of ways in this league … " Coen said after the game. "Just executing that down-and-distance on a fourth down is kind of challenging, especially when they are zero-blitzing every play. The ball's going to come out. It's like a 'hope' play."

So the Jaguars kicked the field goal and the Giants ran out the clock with two first downs. The Giants won 23-18 after leading for the final 47 minutes.

The Jaguars' strategy of relying on their defense during a day their offense struggled to maintain rhythm did not work out for the visiting team. But the strategy worked well to motivate a Giants team that had lost its own rhythm after halftime.

If the Jaguars thought the Giants weren't going to realize the message their field goal sent, they were mistaken. New York quarterback J.J. McCarthy said "as an offense, we took that personal" as Jacksonville hedged on yet another New York implosion.

"100%, it's disrespectful as hell," right tackle Jermaine Eleumenor said from the postgame locker room. "You're kicking a field goal, you think you're going to get a stop on defense, and if I'm being honest, we were whooping them. On the line of scrimmage, they weren't winning. We won the line of scrimmage, both sides of the ball."

On a day in which the Jaguars were down starting center Robert Hainsey (knee) and lost starting left tackle Walker Little (knee) early in the fourth quarter, a pressure-happy Giants defense kept Trevor Lawrence from ever finding a rhythm.

Arvell Reese brings the heat on Trevor Lawrence in the Giants' victory Sunday.

And on a day in which the Jaguars were onboarding their trade-deadline acquisition starting defenders in defensive tackle Jordan Davis and safety Jessie Bates III, the Giants capitalized on a group adjusting to complex schemes, including with quarterback keepers that powered each of their touchdown drives.

So consider the Giants aware that they were 6-point betting underdogs at home and aware that plenty questioned their division-leading record on account of the below-.500 teams they had beaten.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh called his team's sixth victory "the first real football win."

Edge rusher Abdul Carter said "everybody pretty much counted us out."

"But we took that as disrespect, and we came out with a chip on our shoulder…" said Carter, who finished the game with two sacks, five quarterback hits and eight pressures, per Pro Football Focus. "I think we proved that we are worthy. They keep saying we can't beat these teams, we can't beat them. I don't know why they're saying that.

At the end of the first quarter, the Jaguars had not scored a touchdown.

At the end of the second and then third, they hadn't either.

This was a Jacksonville team that entered the week averaging 29.9 points per game, fourth in the league. Its 358.9 yards per game ranked ninth in total offense. So what explained the 20-6 deficit that trickled into the fourth quarter?

"I played really, really poorly today, and you're not going to win many games if I don't play better than that …" said Lawrence, who more than doubled his first three quarters' output with a 164-yard fourth quarter that brought his day to 301 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions on 25-of-47 (53.2%) passing. "As an offense as a whole, I thought we didn't come out with the aggressiveness and attacking that we normally have.

"I felt like they punched us in the mouth a little bit."

Coen blamed himself for some of his early play-calling, saying he overcompensated for run calls he regretted a week prior by calling three straight passes to set up the opening drive's field goal. The Jaguars strayed on multiple drives from their run, which typically sets up their play-action passing and sets the tone for their physical offensive style. On third-and-medium-to-longs, the Giants pressured Lawrence to the tune of turnovers, incompletions and sacks.

Facing third-and-6 with 7:45 to play in the first quarter, Lawrence thought he could hit receiver Parker Washington out of reach of cornerback Deonte Banks before realizing it was "just a really bad read, really bad decision."

With 11:08 to play in the fourth quarter, Lawrence aimed to throw high and early to avoid an approaching defensive lineman, instead throwing to a spot receiver Jakobi Meyers had yet to reach.

The Giants turned the interceptions into six total points on a day they won by five.

Yet when Jacksonville safety Antonio Johnson stripped running back Cam Skattebo and returned the fumble 42 yards, the Jaguars' offense responded with a turnover on downs. Complementary football eluded the team.

By the time Lawrence found a rhythm in the fourth quarter, hitting receiver Brian Thomas Jr. for an 18-yard touchdown on third-and-10 sandwiched between two field-goal drives, the Jaguars' defense was waning. Perhaps matters would have been different if the officials had ruled differently on Washington's fourth-quarter catch in which he got two feet down but didn't secure the ball without movement as he fell to the ground; but even Lawrence admitted: "It was close, and you can't leave it in the ref's hands."

The Giants celebrated holding onto a lead after letting their last contest slip away to the Washington Commanders in the final minute. Lawrence lamented that his offense's rally was too little, too late.

"It was nice to see the fight at the end of the game and that we were still able to have a shot, thanks to our defense," Lawrence said. "We let our defense down today. They got us a bunch of turnovers and gave us plenty of opportunities to win the game, and we didn't capitalize."

At 6-3-1, the Giants maintained their grip on the NFC East even as the Cowboys improved to 5-6 with a 51-30 win over the Tennessee Titans. Next Gen Stats projects the Giants' chances of making the playoffs at 70% after the win.

The Jaguars, meanwhile, don't just remain atop the AFC South at 7-3. Thanks to their three-game lead in the division, they carry a 98% chance of making the playoffs, per Next Gen Stats.

So postseason contention is not a front-of-mind problem. Cleaning up the errors that the Giants exposed, however, is.

Less than two weeks after trading for Davis and Bates as indications of the belief in the 2026 Jaguars, Jacksonville coaches and executives continue to echo that message.

"They believe in this year and they believe that we can make a push to go to the Super Bowl," cornerback Jourdan Lewis told Yahoo Sports. "Those dreams are still intact, just getting accustomed to the guys and how we want to play and how to attack offenses and how they want to attack our system too. …

Instead, the Jaguars will continue working to acclimate Bates to split-safety looks that differ from his Atlanta responsibilities prior to the trade, and they'll work with Davis as he learns the nuances of coordinator Anthony Campanile's movement calls while remembering that gap integrity, physicality and winning in the trenches will always be the foundation for defensive-line success.

The Jaguars were quiet as they shuffled into the postgame locker room from a rainy MetLife Field. But as they showered and packed up for their flight home, their tone reflected focus more than despair.

There are holes to patch. There is time, in the seven remaining regular-season contests, to patch them.

"It's not the end of the world," Davis told Yahoo Sports of Coen's message. "We have to fix the issues. We have to take our medicine. We have to look ourselves in the mirror and then move forward the next week.

"You don't have time to dwell on your wins and losses in the previous week. You have to move on."

So on the Jaguars will move from their five-point loss and on they'll move from Coen's decision to kick a field goal with 3:43 remaining. Jacksonville's offensive players will levy that decision into motivation to show their head coach next time that they're capable of beating blitzes and performing even when the down and distance doesn't favor them.

Jacksonville's defense will translate its inability to get the stop on which Coen relied into motivation to shore up the assignments that ceded McCarthy a 19-yard completion up the middle and Skattebo a 5-yard run on second-and-5 to seal the win.

Several Jaguars players echoed their trust in Coen on that decision and beyond. And Lawrence, who said he struggled to read the field efficiently until late in the game, said he understood which part of those late-game analytics moments were in his control.

"It's not my decision at the end of the day," Lawrence said. "It's coach's, but I stand by him. We've got to make plays on first, second and third down so we have a chance to go for it not on fourth-and-7 or 8. It's just a tough down …

"We know who we are. We just didn't play well tonight. If you don't play well, you get beat."

#2644. Jayson Tatum misses game winner in loss to Warriors as Celtics continue on worst losing skid since 2021

The Boston Celtics, thanks to a big defensive stand from Draymond Green late, are now on their worst losing skid in years.

The Celtics fell to the Golden State Warriors 88-87 on Sunday night at the Chase Center in San Francisco. That was Boston's fourth straight loss, too, which marked the first time that the franchise had lost four consecutive games since May 2021.

They had gone a ridiculous 429 games without a four-game losing skid, which was the second-longest stretch in franchise history. The Celtics once went 468 games from 1962-68.

Boston led by as many as 11 late in the third quarter, and seemed in a great spot to grab the win and limit the damage to three losses. But the Warriors slowly chipped away and got back into the game, and even took the lead on a huge Brandin Podziemski 3-pointer with about 2:30 left in the contest. That was the last points that the Warriors scored.

But with just eight seconds left, Tatum had a great look to win the game. Down by a single point, Tatum drove at Green and took a fadeaway jumper from the elbow over Green. The shot was off the mark, and he finished going 0-of-7 from the field in the second half.

Podziemski led the Warriors with 18 points and seven rebounds in the win, which moved them to 9-8 on the season and ended a five-game losing streak of their own. Charles Bassey added 13 points and nine rebounds, and Green finished with nine points. The Warriors are still missing Stephen Curry, who is sidelined with an abdominal injury.

Tatum finished with 27 points and 10 rebounds while shooting 8-of-20 from the field. Derrick White had 14 points, and Luka Garza added 10 off the bench. They were the only three Celtics players to hit double figures, and the 87 points they managed as a team were the fewest they've scored all season.

It wasn't just Sunday night where they blew a lead, either. Boston had double-digit leads in three of their four losses, including a 17-point lead over the Denver Nuggets before blowing that contest on Wednesday. They were up by 13 points at Sacramento on Saturday, too, before Keegan Murray sank a put-back jumper to seal the one-point win.

Boston got the losing streak started on Monday in a 10-point loss to the Orlando Magic, who rallied late to grab the win at TD Garden.

While the losing streak isn't great, it's far from the time to be concerned for the Celtics. It's not even December yet, and they sit at 11-6 on the season. That's good for third in the Eastern Conference standings, behind only the Philadelphia 76ers and Atlanta Hawks. There is plenty of time for the Celtics to rebound from this stretch and maintain their position in the East. And, the longest losing streak in NBA History is 28 games. The Celtics aren't even close to that mark.

But their run of keeping losing streaks to a minimum has officially come to an end. They'll have a chance to snap the four-game losing skid next on Tuesday night against the Washington Wizards.

#2641. Sean Payton pays tribute to late Tom Jackson with heartwarming gesture after Broncos win

Broncos head coach Sean Payton made a heartwarming gesture toward the family of the late Denver great Tom Jackson following the Broncos' 38-24 win over the Raiders on Sunday.

Payton told reporters after the game that he had presented Jackson's family with the game ball.

Jackson died on Friday with his death being reported publicly on Sunday by ESPN's Adam Schefter.

"I would be remiss if we didn't start with just honoring Tom Jackson tonight," Payton said. "As a coach, you're always teaching and a lot of these players certainly won't remember him as a player, maybe not as an ESPN media member. But [his family] got a game ball tonight. He's part of the rich history. Tough loss for everyone."

Jackson's family notified ESPN of his passing on Friday and no cause of death was revealed.

Jackson, a fourth-round pick by the Broncos back in 1973, played 14 seasons in Denver and appeared in 191 regular-season games and 10 playoff contests.

He then went on to have an impressive 29-year run at ESPN as a staple alongside Chris Berman.

"I knew him more as an ESPN member with Chris Berman, like everyone grew up with that," Payton said. "I felt like I got to know him. Before even coming here [to Denver], and that was in his ESPN role. But when you get here and you learn more about the history of who was coordinating the defense, what position guys were playing, that kind of thing, it's interesting."

The Broncos released a statement earlier on Sunday, mourning the loss of Jackson when the news was announced.

Denver Broncos linebacker Tom Jackson looks on during a game against the Buffalo Bills at Rich Stadium in Orchard Park, N.Y., Oct. 21, 1984. Getty Images

"The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history," the organization said in the statement. "An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos' first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos country.

"TJ's dynamic personality, quick wit and football knowledge made him a natural for television and paved the way for a Hall of Fame broadcasting career. For generations of fans, Tom was an iconic fixture on ESPN's Sunday NFL Countdown and NFL Primetime, sharing his thoughtful insight with an unmistakable sense of humor that defined an era of sports broadcasting.

"Above all, TJ loved the Broncos and was a cherished member of our family for more than 50 years. We extend our deepest sympathies to Tom's wife, Jennifer, his daughters, Taylor and Morgan, and all of his family, friends and teammates."

#2640. Kirk Cousins’ family jumped at the chance to return to Minnesota after Raiders trade

After being traded from the Las Vegas Raiders to the Minnesota Vikings on the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10, 38-year-old quarterback Kirk Cousins said in a press conference that he was hoping his family would come with him to Minnesota. Cousins understood that leaving the kids' school, baseball, and the Las Vegas routine wasn't an easy decision, so the final say was his wife Julie's.

Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) passes the ball during Raiders Training Camp at Intermountain Health Performance Center, Monday Aug. 10, 2026 in Henderson, Nev.

Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) passes the ball during Raiders Training Camp at Intermountain Health Performance Center, Monday Aug. 10, 2026 in Henderson, Nev.

Cousins reminisced about his neighbors and the atmosphere in Minnesota, saying he loved Minnesota so much that there was no reason to leave, and when people talk about "Minnesota Nice," he experiences it every day with his neighbors.

Julie picked up her two sons, 9-year-old Cooper and 7-year-old Turner, from school and baseball/little league and laid out the options in front of them: Dad got traded to the Vikings, so do they want to stay in Las Vegas or go with Dad to Minnesota? Even though they liked spending a little time in Sin City (Las Vegas), both kids immediately said without hesitation, "Let's go!" NBC sideline reporter Melissa Stark shared on the 'Sunday Night Football' broadcast that Julie told her the whole family wanted to embrace this new adventure, and the kids' immediate answer meant a lot to Kirk.

Earlier, on the Netflix documentary series "Quarterback," one of their sons had also asked Julie on a trip to Minnesota, "When are we getting our house back?"

Within just a few hours of the trade deal being finalized, the whole family had packed their suitcases. After playing one last little league playoff game, Turner set off back to Minnesota, hunting for his old Vikings jerseys, where Cousins had already played 6 seasons from 2018 to 2023.

Minnesota Vikings, who were 6-2, needed an experienced player urgently after Kyler Murray's hamstring injury and Carson Wentz's poor performance to try to save their season and Super Bowl hopes after two straight losses.

On Nov. 10, the Vikings got Cousins back from the Raiders in exchange for a 2027 third-round draft pick. Under the deal, the Vikings took on the responsibility to pay Cousins his remaining $650,000 salary for the 2026 season and a $10 million roster bonus for the next year, while Cousins had thrown for 2,340 passing yards and 20 touchdowns in the first 9 games of the 2026 season with the Raiders.

This season, combining money from 3 teams (Falcons $8.7 million, Raiders ~ $650,000, and Vikings ~ $650,000), he's getting around $10 million in total. After playing 6 seasons with the Vikings from 2018 to 2023, Cousins joined the Atlanta Falcons in March 2024 on a $180 million deal and the Las Vegas Raiders in April 2026 on an $11.3 million deal.

At Lambeau Field stadium, where he had torn his Achilles tendon (in his leg) on October 29, 2023, Cousins led the Vikings to a big 30-10 win over the Green Bay Packers on Nov. 15, completing 21 of 31 passes for 207 passing yards and 2 touchdowns.

After the game, during an ESPN interview, he got emotional remembering the tough times of the past 3 years and said, "There's more to the story being written."

In his second start with Minnesota, on Nov. 22 in Mexico City, he threw for 235 yards but no touchdowns and an interception in a 35-10 loss to the 49ers.

Cousins and his family really love Minnesota's four seasons, having bonfires in the backyard, and their neighbors, who happily shovelled the snow outside their house. They were really fond of their old quiet suburban cul-de-sac street, which had a peaceful North Woods vibe, and the Vikings' practice facility and airport were also nearby.

A local friend shared that, "They want to get back to a time where they can go and have a bonfire in a backyard."

"That was Kirk's big thing after games. He'd just sit out there after the kids go to bed and replay the whole game in his head."

With the trade done, the family's next task is finding a place to live. After returning to the team, the family is getting everything set up from scratch, and for now, the whole family is staying in a hotel while Julie looks for a new home. Cousins laughed and said that first, they need a driveway because they don't have one right now, so they're taking things day by day.

#2630. MLB rumors: Blue Jays targeting Ketel Marte, Giants rejecting trade calls for ace Logan Webb

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with two significant transactions. The Braves signed reliever Evan Phillips (three years and $35 million) and the Red Sox signed slugger Jake Bauers (four years and $58 million). Bauers will give Boston some sorely needed home run power. Phillips will pair with Robert Suarez in the late innings for Atlanta.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Saturday's hot stove happenings.

The Blue Jays have interest in Diamondbacks second baseman Ketel Marte, who has a full no-trade protection, reports Sportsnet. It does not appear a trade is imminent. We ranked Marte among the offseason's top trade candidates despite his odd AWOL incidents the last few seasons. Even at 33, he remains one of the game's best second basemen.

The Blue Jays went 79-83 this past season largely because of their offense, which ranked dead last in runs and home runs. They also ranked 17th in WAR at second base as All-Star Ernie Clement ran out of steam in the second half. Offensively, Marte is coming off his worst 162-game season since 2018, though he would still represent a clear upgrade for the Blue Jays.

The Giants continue to decline trade calls about ace righty Logan Webb, reports USA Today. Webb, 30 next week, had his worst full season in the big leagues in 2026, in part due to a nagging knee injury, though he is signed affordably through 2028. San Francisco needs to add to its rotation, not subtract one of the game's best and most durable starters.

That said, a Webb trade would presumably net the Giants multiple young players and improve the team's talent base. It never hurts to listen, but for now, the Giants seem disinclined to move their best pitcher since Madison Bumgarner was in his prime. Webb and Landen Roupp are the only locks for San Francisco's 2027 rotation at the moment.

Not surprisingly, the Braves want to add at least one starting pitcher, according to The Athletic. They could also re-sign Raisel Iglesias or bring in another late-inning reliever even after signing Phillips. Chris Sale and Grant Holmes are Atlanta's only returning healthy starters. Bryce Elder (knee), Spencer Schwellenbach (elbow) and Spencer Strider (elbow) all finished the season injured.

The Braves will give Didier Fuentes, who was so dominant as a reliever this past season, a chance to start in 2027. It will be difficult to count on him for a full season, however. Fuentes, 21, threw a career-high 97 innings between the minors, majors, and postseason in 2026. Atlanta will need to monitor his workload next year. Another starter to soak up innings is a must this offseason.

The Tigers have interest in free agent left-hander Shota Imanaga, reports MLB.com. Jackson Jobe, Troy Melton, River Ryan, and Framber Valdez are presumably locks for Detroit's rotation. Ty Madden and Keider Montero are depth options. Reese Olson is expected back from shoulder surgery early next year. Still, the Tigers could clearly use another starting pitcher.

We ranked Imanaga, 33, as the 30th-best free agent available this offseason. He has been very home run prone the last two years (1.9 homers per nine innings), which could make him a good match for what is now called Fifth Third Park. Detroit's stadium tends to play pitcher-friendly, particularly in April and September (and October), when the ball doesn't carry well in the cold.

The Blue Jays are receiving calls about infielder Ernie Clement and utility man Davis Schneider, reports The Athletic. Teams have also inquired about catcher Brandon Valenzuela, who was a Gold Glove finalist as a rookie in 2026. Toronto reportedly has interest in Jazz Chisholm Jr. as it seeks more of a power bat on the infield, potentially making Clement expendable.

Schneider, 27, had a poor 2026 and spent time in Triple-A, though he is versatile and has hit lefties in spots over the years. There is a shocking shortage of quality right-handed bats throughout baseball right now. Schneider's heavy plate discipline approach and ability to play left field as well as some infield positions make him an interesting enough target this offseason.

The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox are among several teams pursuing Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Taira, 26, had a 1.36 ERA in 145 innings for the Seibu Lions in 2026. We ranked him as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason, though he could ultimately wind up in the bullpen given his height (5-foot-8).

The Padres and two Chicago teams need starting pitching this offseason (they need multiple starters, really) and would likely use Taira in their rotation, at least to begin the season. For what it's worth, Taira told Sanspo he does not have a preferred destination, geographically. The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox would all give him a chance to pitch for a contender right away.

The Cardinals have declined trade inquiries into first baseman Alec Burleson and shortstop Masyn Winn, according to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. St. Louis is also receiving interest in catchers Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pagés, who are more likely to be traded. Burleson and Winn are off-limits, though, and considered part of the long-term future in St. Louis.

Leo Bernal, who was so impressive during his September call up, and top prospect Rainiel Rodriguez are the future behind the plate for the Cardinals. Pagés is a traditional glove-first backup catcher. Crooks has some offensive upside thanks to his hard-hit ability (exit velocity, etc.), and he rates well as a pitch-framer and thrower. He's an appealing target for catcher-needy teams.

The former All-Pro did most of his work near the line of scrimmage, and one of his two explosive plays ended in disaster when he inexplicably carried the ball in one hand and had it punched out, ending a drive to open the second half that could've cut San Francisco's lead to 11. From a purely fantasy perspective, however, it was another step in the right direction as Jefferson has now logged 16 catches for 160 yards in two games with Kirk Cousins -- in his other seven games, he averaged 56 yards on 4.4 receptions per game. He's producing like a decent WR2 now and is on the right path to regaining his usual WR1 status.

This season's NBA Rookie of the Year race has the potential to be one of the closest in league history. While there is no 65-game requirement to win the award — unlike MVP, Defensive Player of the Year and All-NBA honors — playing as many games as possible will be paramount this season in order to claim Rookie of the Year.

That's why Chicago Bulls forward Caleb Wilson faces an uphill climb to win the honor after fracturing his right hand earlier this month. Wilson is set to miss the next 3-5 weeks and will likely lose serious ground to others in his class. He currently has the sixth-best odds (+4000) on FanDuel Sportsbook to win Rookie of the Year.

During the first month of the season, three players have separated themselves at the top: Yaxel Lendeborg, Cameron Boozer, and Darius Acuff Jr. While it's not a guarantee one of those players wins it, if the season ended today, those would be the top vote-getters.

Darryn Peterson and AJ Dybantsa — the first two picks of the 2026 NBA Draft — have some ground to make up during the next four months to get back in the mix.

With the regular season almost a quarter of the way complete, let's dive into our first Rookie of the Year rankings. All odds via FanDuel.

With Steph Curry out, Lendeborg has continued to step up. The oldest player drafted in the first round is coming off a lackluster showing against the Spurs in the NBA Cup, but before that he had three straight games of 23+ points. He is shooting 48.6% from the field and 41.4% from 3. Lendeborg didn't start shooting 3s on a consistent basis until he got to Michigan last season, so knocking down that percentage on 5.4 attempts per night is a positive sign. Fourteen games into the season, Lendeborg is the favorite.

Boozer's raw stats aren't as good as Lendeborg's or even Acuff's, but his impact goes well beyond the box score. His feel for the game is elite for a 19-year-old. Boozer keeps getting better and better as a processor as he continues to log more minutes. The Grizzlies have been one of the league's surprising teams this season. Boozer deserves a ton of credit for that. He wins everywhere he goes, whether at the high school, college, or professional level.

Acuff just turned 20 last week. In 13 games as a teenager, he averaged 25.5 points per game and became the first teenager in NBA history to score at least 275 points and dish out 80 assists in his first 11 games. Acuff is a special offensive talent who is being asked to do more than any rookie in his class. Sacramento is a very bad basketball team, but Acuff makes the Kings somewhat fun to watch. That's a huge credit to him.

The Jazz have been decimated by injuries this season and are currently riding a 12-game losing streak. The one bright side amidst some very bad basketball is how good Peterson has been during that stretch. Peterson had a five-game stretch in which he scored 20 points in each game and shot the ball well from 3. Peterson is the future of Utah's franchise, so getting him as many reps as possible on and off the ball should be the priority.

Dybantsa, the No. 1 overall pick, is averaging 14 shot attempts per game during his first 10 appearances as a pro. He should be taking even more shots. The way the Wizards are using him is confusing at times. Dybantsa is in somewhat of a weird situation because of the Wizards' roster. Washington handed Trae Young a huge contract this offseason that is already aging poorly. Dybantsa should be the focus of the offense. He should be touching the ball and shooting it even more than he is already. I have been impressed with Dybantsa's defense this season.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2626. What's next for Red Sox after Jake Bauers deal? Plus more intel from the MLB GM Meetings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings. The looming lockout, of course, played a major role in all of this.

With Dec. 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place? What will it look like once it returns? How do you build a roster with such indeterminacy?

For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.

Tuesday (Nov. 17) is a significant date, marking the deadline for teams to decide which players to protect from the Rule 5 draft by adding them to their 40-man roster. Campbell, who did not appear in a big-league game in 2026, is currently on the 40-man, signing an eight-year $60 million extension just eight games into his 2025 rookie campaign. But after his demotion in late June of that season, Campbell never found his way back to the majors.

Now, with the lockout upon baseball, according to one source familiar with the situation, Campbell's 40-man spot might be in jeopardy.

Boston is weighing the possibility of designating Campbell for assignment. When Craig Breslow, the Sox's president of baseball operations, was asked about that Tuesday, he brushed aside the question.

"I'm not going to speak to that right now," he said "Kristian's part of our organization. We're really happy about that, and we are invested in doing everything we can to get him to perform like he's capable of."

Now, if the Red Sox do DFA Campbell, the belief is that he would clear waivers, given his contract and lackluster performance at the minor-league level. Campbell is owed $55 million over the next six seasons, earning $13 million and $16 million over the 2031 and 2032 seasons, respectively. Campbell posted a .256/.383/.380 slash line with eight homers in 462 plate appearances at Triple-A in 2026.

Because of those figures, one league executive suggested during the GM Meetings that their club would have no interest in Campbell. The exec took it a step further, confidently suggesting that they couldn't envision any team claiming the outfielder, considering the contract.

Hypothetically, if Campbell is DFA'd, the Red Sox would free up a 40-man roster spot. If he clears waivers, Campbell, who has less than a year of MLB service time, would be outrighted to Triple-A Worcester. The Red Sox could then eventually add him back to the 40-man roster once they feel his production is worthy of another promotion to the parent club.

None of this would provide the Red Sox with any financial relief unless another team were to claim him. Campbell's contract would still count toward their competitive balance tax payroll even if he were removed from the 40-man roster and remained in the minors.

The risk-reward of such a move is something the Red Sox will also have to consider. Campbell has already acknowledged losing confidence following his recent struggles at both the major- and minor-league levels.

"He's got a world of potential," said Breslow. "We saw it in the minor leagues when he was coming up. We saw it in the first part of the season in [2025]. Then I think we started to see it in the second half last year, too, [at Worcester]. I still feel like he has a really bright big-league career ahead of him, and excited to get into spring training and see that manifest on the field."

The Red Sox signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal Friday, giving the club another power bat in their lineup. Willson Contreras will continue to anchor first base while Bauers will serve as the primary DH, filling in for Contreras from time to time.

Bauers had a breakout season with the Brewers this year, batting .266/.389/.484 with an .874 OPS and 26 homers. The combo of plate discipline and damage in the strike zone intrigued the Red Sox. Furthermore, his ability to lift the ball in the air and use the entire field despite being a lefty gives the Red Sox confidence that he will be productive at Fenway.

With Bauers part of the fold, though, Jarren Duran's future with the club is even more murky. The Sox are a heavily left-handed offensive club with Bauers, Wilyer Abreu, Masataka Yoshida, Roman Anthony, and Duran in the mix.

One is likely going to have to go. And Duran, who could earn upwards of $11 million in arbitration next season, appears to be the most likely to be dealt.

Even before the Bauers signing, multiple sources suggested during the GM Meetings that both the Red Sox and Duran might be better off parting ways via trade.

"I've been hearing for three years now about the outfield logjam that we have, but the reality is we haven't had all of our outfielders, including Masataka, healthy at the same time," Breslow said. "These things have largely taken care of themselves, unfortunately."

#2624. LeBron James denies report that he asked 76ers for 'patience' with scoring numbers at career low

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia 76ers are off to a fantastic start to the 2026-27 season at 12-3, good for first in the Eastern Conference, and perhaps most encouraging for the Sixers is that they're winning without looking like a team playing at its absolute peak.

After a huge offseason adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, the Sixers still look like a team figuring out how best to work together, but when it comes time in the fourth quarter to find a way to win, they manage to get the job done. Tyrese Maxey is leading the way with Brown quickly finding his rhythm, but James and Joel Embiid in particular still seem to be feeling it out early in the season.

James, who has never averaged less than 20.9 points per game in his previous 23 seasons, is averaging just 15.1 points per game and his 44.3/22.5/71.7 shooting splits are all career lows or close to it. As James figures things out, ESPN reported that a Sixers source claimed James "asked coaches to be patient with him as he expects to find his rhythm and get his conditioning in line by December as he ramps up."

That report hit social media and caught James' attention, with the 41-year-old star denying ever saying that.

ESPN didn't report a direct quote from James, and it's very possible the Sixers source offered an anecdote that paraphrased James and used the word patience when James never did. That then ended up on a social media graphic and prompted James to shoot it down.

What's fascinating here is it's not a scathing report or even anything particularly juicy. James is struggling with his shot early in the year and seems to be figuring out exactly where he fits in the offense alongside Maxey, Brown and Embiid as a scorer. He's still doing plenty of things well -- including leading the team with 6.9 assists per game and just took over third all-time in assists in NBA history -- and the Sixers are still winning even with James ice cold with his jumper, which history suggests will turn around at some point.

Patience would be prudent from the Sixers with James, whether he wants to use that word or not, and it seems like a matter of when, not if, he gets shots to start falling and the Philly offense becomes even more dynamic.

With the General Manager Meetings now in the rearview mirror, it sure seems like we're playing out the clock in Major League Baseball news until the CBA expires. That would be Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET. The expectation at this juncture is that the owners will lock the players out and we'll deal with several months of public negotiations. Until then, we can hope to see some player movement, such as the Red Sox signing Jake Bauers.

In the meantime, let's round up the news and rumors for the day.

The Padres are in desperate need of starting pitching, should they wish to continue contending. The rotation right now would be Joe Musgrove, Randy Vásquez, JP Sears, Jhony Brito and a shrugging emoji. Sure enough, they are all over the rumor mill for rotation help.

The San Diego Union-Tribune reports that they've shown interest in "virtually every starting pitcher" in free agency, "from Tarik Skubal on down. From Matthew Boyd to Shota Imanaga to Dustin May to Kaima Taira." Further, ESPN reports that the Padres have a meeting set up with Skubal but have also shown interest in Freddy Peralta, as well as Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Nick Martinez.

Expect them to remain active until they land at least two starters.

It's no secret that the Diamondbacks are open to trading All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte. The Blue Jays have been sniffing around, and now the Orioles have emerged as a suitor, per MLB.com.

This one is interesting in that it's not a natural fit. The Orioles have extra infielders and have been said to be shopping infielders in order to land outfield help. Between second and third base, the Orioles have Jackson Holliday, Jordan Westburg, Blaze Alexander, Coby Mayo and Christian Encarnacion-Strand. Presumably, if they are able to swing a deal for Marte, there would be some shuffling with more trades and/or moving someone to the outfield.

The Mets could have an opening at first base as things currently stand and they've checked in on free agent Ty France, according to the New York Post.

Currently, the Mets are looking at Jared Young (coming off a scary head injury), Mark Vientos and Jorge Polanco as options at first base.

France, 32 and probably considered a journeyman at this point, had a big season in 2026 for the Padres. He hit .295/.363/.502 (139 OPS+) with 21 homers, 72 RBI and a career-high 4.5 WAR.

Reliever Jonathan Loáisiga is close to signing with a new team, reports ESPN. The Dodgers are among five teams involved, with the New York Post adding the Phillies, Mets, Yankees and Blue Jays to the mix.

In 67 outings last season for Arizona, Loáisiga pitched to a 2.42 ERA, 1.03 WHIP and had 48 strikeouts in 67 innings.

The Yankees have re-signed left-handed reliever Tim Hill to a one-year, $2.25 million deal with a $2.5 million club option for 2028, per ESPN. Hill, 36, made 67 appearances last season with a 4.60 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 25 strikeouts in 58 ⅔ innings. He held lefties to a .213/.265/.346 line.
